name: Ma'a
catalog_citation: Thomason, Sarah G. 1983. Genetic relationship and the case of Ma'a (Mbugu). Studies in African Linguistics 14(2): 195-231.
catalog_locator: p. 204 (sec. 2.1, phonology; PDF page 10 of the saved file)
catalog_quote: Ma'a has lost the contrast between long and short vowels that characterizes most Cushitic languages, including Proto-SC. ... As for prosodic features, Ma'a has two phonemic tones and predictable stress on the first stem syllable [Ehret, p.c. 1982]. According to Ehret, Bantu loanwords contributed to the development of tone in Ma'a; he does not reconstruct lexical tone phonemes for Proto-SC, and he considers Iraqw to have neither phonemic tone nor phonemic stress [p.c. 1982]. Dahalo, like Ma'a, has lexical tone distinctions. In general, Cushitic languages have phonemic stress, while Bantu languages have phonemic tones.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ma'a/Mbugu is a two-tone (H/L) language; stress is non-contrastive and predictable, falling on the first syllable of the stem (i.e. stem-initial, after any noun-class or verbal prefixes). This stress claim is reported by Thomason from Christopher Ehret's personal communication (1982), not from her own fieldwork. The primary modern grammar (Mous 2003, sec. 4.5 p.104; Mous 2013 APiCS) describes only tone (two register tones, distinctive on every syllable of noun roots; verb roots lexically H or L) and makes no statement about stress anywhere in the book (verified by full-text search-inside).
new_statements.exceptions: None; Thomason gives no examples or exceptions for the stress placement. Mous 2003 notes H-tone spreading to the penultimate in certain verb forms (pp.109-110), a tonal, not stress, phenomenon.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level claim ('first stem syllable'), morphologically anchored to the stem rather than the prefixed word; no phrase-level discussion. Applies to Ma'a (Inner Mbugu); Mous treats Inner and Normal Mbugu as one phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Thomason's statement concerns Ma'a (= Inner Mbugu, the mixed lect with Cushitic/para-lexicon); Mous 2003/2013 treat Inner Mbugu (Ma'á) and Normal Mbugu (the Pare-like Bantu lect) as sharing one phonology and grammar. Glottolog mbug1240 covers both under 'Mbugu' (ISO mhd). Glottolog's ref 'Gil & Shen 2019 Frontiers in Psychology' listed as a grammar is unrelated to Mbugu (mis-tagged).

sources.citation: Mous, Maarten. 2003. The Making of a Mixed Language: The case of Ma'a/Mbugu (Creole Language Library 26). Amsterdam: John Benjamins. Ch. 4 Phonology (pp. 95-110), sec. 4.5 Tone p.104.
sources.access_detail: read online, no file saved; access check: publisher record (DOI); no open copy and no library e-access found (also: publisher (doi, likely paywalled))
sources.note: Google Books partial preview: page images of pp.57, 95-97, 99, 101, 103-105, 107-108, 110 saved and scanned. Sec. 4.5 (p.104): two tones H/L, tone distinctive on every syllable of nouns, verb roots lexically H or L; contour tones = sequences on disyllabic long vowels. Chapter intro (p.95) lists tone as the only suprasegmental unit. Full-text search-inside of the whole book: 'stress' occurs only pp.48, 57 ('not... utterance final reduction, related to stress or tone'), 120 (none a stress rule); 'accent' only p.104 (acute accent = H tone). No statement on word stress anywhere in the book.
